# Radar (`radar`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/electricity.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Electricity & electronics (`electricity`)
- Deps: needs electromagnetic_waves_radio, vacuum_tube; helped by television_crt, crystal_detector, speed_of_light
- Core idea: Radio waves are reflected by metal objects, ships, aircraft and coastlines. Send a very short, powerful pulse, about a millionth of a second, and time the echo on a cathode-ray tube: the waves cover 300 m in a microsecond, so each microsecond of delay means 150 m of range. A narrow beam, turned to find the strongest echo, gives the direction, and the beam is narrow only if the aerial is many wavelengths wide, which is why wavelengths of centimetres are wanted. The cavity magnetron, a copper block with resonant holes round a hot cathode in a strong magnetic field, produces such waves at kilowatt power; a silicon point-contact crystal detects the weak echo.
- Pitfalls:
  - Explaining it as a single brilliant invention; it was developed in secret in at least eight countries in the 1930s, and Britain's lead lay in the reporting and fighter-control system built round it
  - Using a continuous wave and wondering how to measure distance; the pulse and its timing are the essential idea
  - Forgetting that the received echo falls with the fourth power of the distance, so doubling the range needs sixteen times the power
  - Standing in front of a powerful microwave aerial; the beam heats tissue, especially the eyes
- History: europe: 1904 – Hülsmeyer's Telemobiloskop detects ships by reflected waves (Cologne, no buyers); February 1935 Watson-Watt and Wilkins' Daventry experiment; 1937–1939 Chain Home stations; 1934–1939 German Freya and Würzburg sets; February 1940 Randall and Boot's cavity magnetron (Birmingham); americas: 1922, 1930 – US Naval Research Laboratory notes reflections from ships and aircraft; 1934–1936 Page's pulse radar; 1940 the Tizard mission brings the magnetron to the United States, MIT Radiation Laboratory and Bell Labs mass-produce microwave radar; east_asia: 1927 – Okabe's split-anode magnetron (Tohoku University); Japanese military radar from 1941
- Read:
  - Robert Buderi, The Invention That Changed the World (1996)
  - Louis Brown, A Radar History of World War II: Technical and Military Imperatives (1999)
